faqs.question: What is tax-loss harvesting?
faqs.answer: Tax-loss harvesting is the practice of selling an investment that has declined in value to realize a capital loss, then using that loss to offset capital gains recognized elsewhere in your portfolio. Any loss beyond what is needed to offset gains can also offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year, with the remainder carried forward indefinitely to future tax years.

faqs.question: What are the tax-loss harvesting rules I need to know?
faqs.answer: The most important rule is the wash-sale rule: if you sell a security at a loss and buy the same security, or one the IRS considers substantially identical, within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss is disallowed and instead added to the cost basis of the replacement shares. Losses must also first offset gains of the same character, short-term losses against short-term gains and long-term against long-term, before offsetting the other type, and only $3,000 of net losses can offset ordinary income in a given year, with any excess carried forward.

faqs.question: How is direct indexing different from investing in an index fund?
faqs.answer: An index fund pools your money with other investors to buy all the securities in an index inside one fund share, so you can only realize a gain or loss on the fund as a whole. Direct indexing buys the individual underlying stocks directly in your own account, which means each stock has its own cost basis. That structure allows losses to be harvested company by company, sometimes even in a year when the overall index is flat or positive, which is not possible when you hold a single pooled fund position.

faqs.question: Does tax-loss harvesting guarantee better after-tax returns?
faqs.answer: No. Tax-loss harvesting can improve after-tax returns in years when there is meaningful dispersion among individual holdings and available losses to harvest, but the outcome depends on market conditions, account size, and tax bracket, and it involves added trading activity and cost compared to a simple index fund. In years when a market or index rises steadily with little dispersion, there may be few or no losses available to harvest. It is a tax-efficiency tool, not a guaranteed source of additional return, and results vary by individual circumstances.
